headline: 10 Days After Fatal Building Collapse, a Brooklyn Block Is in Limbo

paragraphs.text: Ciahola Lawrence became a U.S. citizen in 2014, after years of living in New York City as an unauthorized immigrant. Few possessions are as precious to her as the papers, like her Social Security card, that prove her legal status.
Ms. Lawrence, 54, tucked them carefully in a folder under the couch in her third-floor Brooklyn apartment, along with other mementos, like her junior high school diploma.
She might never see those items again.

Last week, the building next to hers collapsed, leaving eight people dead and 18 others injured, and displacing Ms. Lawrence and more than a dozen of her neighbors in Flatbush, a bustling working-class area that is home to many immigrants. As officials investigate what went wrong, other residents of the block have been kept from returning, left to wonder about their futures and whether their homes are also in danger.

The collapse, at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, sheared off a wall of the adjoining building, leaving its apartments open to the air. City officials say they now must demolish that building, 1323 Flatbush, where Ms. Lawrence and her husband had lived for six years.

To make matters worse, nobody — not even city officials or engineers — will be allowed to enter the building, because of potential asbestos contamination and structural instability, the city’s Buildings Department said. That means that Ms. Lawrence’s immigration papers, and everything else in her apartment, may be lost forever.
“I want people to know that my home was special,” she said. “I want people to know that I worked hard for everything that I had in there.”

It is not clear when 1323 Flatbush will be torn down. But to prevent a possible domino effect on the block, where several aging buildings stand side by side, the city said it was installing supports in the next building over — 1325 Flatbush — this week. Both that building, which currently has no tenants, and the one on its other side, 1327 Flatbush, remain under vacate orders.

The city is working to assist the people who have been displaced. Thirteen households have been relocated to hotels, according to the city, until at least the end of the month. The city’s housing department is helping to find permanent homes for residents of the collapsed building and the one next door. City officials said that displaced residents and the families of those killed or injured in the collapse had been given a total of $60,000 in gift cards to help pay for food and other necessities.
Still, residents said they felt like they were in limbo.
“There was no time to get belongings back,” said Moussa Keita, 44, another resident of 1323 Flatbush. Mr. Keita was at work in New Jersey at the time of the collapse.
He said he was frustrated that he could not return to his apartment to retrieve his wife’s passport, family photos and important paperwork before the building was demolished.
“Why do they care about safety now?” he said of buildings officials. “Why didn’t they care about safety before?”

Ahmed Tigani, the buildings commissioner, said in a statement this week announcing the demolition plan that the “entire administration will continue to support the tenants displaced by this incredible tragedy and help the neighborhood, and our entire city, recover.”

While neighbors contend with the aftermath of the disaster, officials are conducting safety sweeps at some 160 sites across the city associated with people or companies that have ties to the collapse.

A visual analysis by The New York Times this week found that 1321 Flatbush — a three-story, century-old, mixed-use building — most likely fell because the excavation at a construction site next door weakened its foundation.

The nature of the collapse made it extremely likely that the building next door, with its peeled-off wall, would have to come down, said Chris Cerino, a structural engineer and former president of the Structural Engineers Association of New York.
“You were looking into it like a dollhouse,” he said. “There’s no way to save that.”
What wasn’t immediately clear at the time of the disaster was that the building was in such bad shape that residents would not be able to retrieve their belongings.

Andrew Rudansky, a Buildings Department spokesman, said the condition of the building had deteriorated in the days after the collapse and that the city had begun informing residents on Tuesday that it was not safe to enter.
Before the building is torn down, though, the department must shore up its other neighbor, 1325 Flatbush.

That is because the two structures share load-bearing walls called “party walls,” a common type of construction in New York City, Mr. Cerino said. Securing the stability of 1325 could involve separating the floors of 1323 from the shared party wall. Then, the city would need to monitor vibrations and movements along the entire chain of buildings on Flatbush before, during and after demolition.
“They are very brittle buildings,” Mr. Cerino said.
The deadly collapse has prompted a criminal investigation and citywide alarm about the stability of buildings near construction sites. The displaced Flatbush residents have more immediate concerns.
Michael Williams, 50, a resident of 1323 Flatbush, said he was worried about where he would live when the Red Cross stopped paying for his temporary housing.
“Don’t put us in your shelter,” he said.

DeAndre Finley, 28, was forced to leave 1327 Flatbush after the collapse and has been living in a hotel. He said he was told that if he was not allowed back into his apartment by the end of the month, he would be moved to a shelter.

But the situation has created a conundrum, he said: He doesn’t want to move back into his building, but the landlord doesn’t seem keen to let him out of his lease. And he worries that even when the building has been deemed safe, it might not remain so.
Why, Mr. Finley asked, would I want to live next to a building that collapsed and another that is about to be demolished?
“And we’re the last building that isn’t?” he said. “No way.”
